title: Weird query performance - optimize query execution
body:
Most resent Neo4j AuraDB

I found that Neo4j executes some simple queries in a very strange way. E.g. the most simple case:
```
MATCH p=(a)-[*]->(b:LABEL3) WHERE b.property = 'test'
    and (a:LABEL1 OR a:LABEL2)
RETURN p
```

will filter all labels first and make a Cartesian product -> this is far from optimal. (and will almost never finish on huge graphs)


Instead of 
```
MATCH p=(a)-[*]->(b:LABEL3) WHERE b.property = 'test'
RETURN p
```

This will filter on the target node and return all paths. This is executed in an instant.

Neo4j should consider moving the "Filter" clause to the end of the execution plan in this case.
The current workaround is using the second query and filtering the labels in my own code (after I got the result), as the first query will execute forever.

comments.author: reporter
comments.body:
In addition:
`MATCH p=(a)-[*]->(b:LABEL3) WHERE b.property = 'test'
    and (a:LABEL1 OR a:LABEL2)
RETURN p LIMIT 25`
With a limit clause, it does exactly what is proposed above. 

So there is an issue as soon as a certain threshold is reached and it starts using a way less efficient cartesian product.

comments.author: participant1
comments.body:
Hello @reporter, 

Thank you for reaching out to us and reporting this issue. 

The query planner will generate many different ways of solving the same query, and will perform a cost-based comparison between each of these ways. In order to do this, it looks at the operators in each query (cartesian product, filter, etc) as well as statistics about the current state of the database which will contain information such as how many nodes of label LABEL1 exist on disk.

It could well be that based on the statistics of the current of the database, the plan with the cartesian product is the most optimal. Such a plan might indeed scale poorly if the state of the database was to significantly change, but the database is able to detect such scenarios and would force a the query to be recompiled (the new plan would probably not contain a cartesian product).

Generally speaking, cartesian product may be cheap to execute if one or both sides of the cartesian product have very few records which might be the case if the right and left hand side operators of the cartesian product are very selective (eg NodeByLabelScan).

If you would like to pursue this issue further, then would you mind please prefixing your queries with `debug=printcostcomparisons` and sending us the output you see in your `neo4j.log` file? I will then ask a team member to have a look and get back to you.

```
CYPHER debug=printcostcomparisons
EXPLAIN
MATCH p=(a)-[*]->(b:LABEL3) 
WHERE b.property = 'test'
      AND a:LABEL1 OR a:LABEL2
RETURN p
```

Hope you have a nice day

(I know AxB≠BxA but in the Neo4j case above it's basically a bijective cartesian product)

comments.author: participant2
comments.body:
Hi @reporter,

Thank you for coming back to this and sorry that retrieval of the graph counts is not available in Aura Free. I can see two topics in this issue, so I will address them individually:

## Order of the Cartesian product

It looks to me like there are far fewer relationships we need to traverse from `t` for finding the paths. This could for example be because `u` is more connected than `t` such as in this simplified sketch:
![Untitled graph(2)](https://github.com/neo4j/neo4j/assets/79841228/c5b3b897-a08d-423d-86d0-3f1f9ea7cb44)

That should explain why one plan performs a lot better than the other.

## Getting a linear plan

In the original post, you wrote that

```Cypher
MATCH p=(a)-[*]->(b:LABEL3) WHERE b.property = 'test'
RETURN p
```

performs better as it produces a linear plan and does not use a Cartesian product.

Usually, it helps giving the planner more information on the relationships, such as applying relationship types. That way, it may become better at estimating when a Cartesian product is preferable to a linear plan.

In case, you cannot make it work, you can "force" the planner by introducing a `WITH * SKIP 0` to separate the parts of the query which should be solved first and which after that:

```Cypher
MATCH p=(a)-[*]->(b:LABEL3) WHERE b.property = 'test'
WITH * SKIP 0 WHERE a:LABEL1|LABEL2
RETURN p
```

This should lead to a linear plan.

## Conclusion

Without looking at your data in more detail, there is not much more I can help you tweak the query. But I hope this will provide you with the necessary tools you need to get the performance that you want.

Let me know if there is more I can help you with.

comments.author: reporter
comments.body:
Wow thanks for our response the 
`WITH * SKIP 0 WHERE a:LABEL1|LABEL2`
did the trick. 

this is a huge difference the "problem" query now executes in milliseconds and even the "working" query is now faster.
pretty interesting the query optimizer doesn't plan this way and isn't using this path.

beside this, I would also say even if:
> It looks to me like there are far fewer relationships we need to traverse from t for finding the paths. 

this should be automatically recognized by the query optimizer (neo4j internally).
so it automatically selects the optimal execution plan (e.g. query in one or another direction depending on what is more efficient)

**so although we have a workaround now, I still think this needs to be properly addressed**:
As any Neo4j User wants the same and most optimal query performance (no matter which direction he writes the query - as they are interchangeable and it's the query optimizers job to find the best/fastest path)

comments.author: participant2
comments.body:
Hi @reporter,

Good to hear that this solved your issue. I do agree that in general, the perfect plan should be chosen.

However, there are cases, where we have too little information on the pattern that the user is looking for to generate an appropriate plan. Keeping track on all possible patterns is equivalent to caching the database: For each pair of `u` and `t` we would need to remember how many paths there are of a certain kind between the two.

To investigate whether we could have been smarter in this particular case, we would the graph counts that I mentioned earlier. I understand that this is not possible for you to produce via the procedure. But if we should investigate, maybe you could send me the details from:

```
COUNT { () }
```

```
MATCH (n)
UNWIND labels(n) AS label
RETURN label, count(*)
```

```
MATCH ()-[r]->()
RETURN type(r), count(*)
```

```
MATCH (a)-[r]->()
UNWIND labels(a) AS label
WITH label, type(r) as relType
RETURN [label, relType], count(*);
```

```
MATCH ()-[r]->(a)
UNWIND labels(a) AS label
WITH label, type(r) as relType
RETURN [relType, label], count(*);
```

That might give us enough clues about what the optimizer's decisions are in your case.
